H1.text: Sodium is stored under kerosene. Chlorine is used to clean drinking water. Neon glows in a sign, but almost never reacts.

H2.text: Three elements with three very different personalities. Yet one map predicts all three.

H3.text: Aarav stops at the periodic table on his college notice board.

H4.text: Sodium sits at the far left. Chlorine sits near the far right. Neon sits at the very end.

H5.text: By the end of this video, you will read five trends off this one table, and know why the two ends react the most.

P1.text: So what is a periodic trend?

P2.text: A trend is a property that changes steadily as you move across a period, or down a group.

P3.text: Across a period, the nucleus gains protons, but the new electrons go into the same shell. The pull grows, and atoms shrink.

P4.text: Down a group, a new shell is added each time. The outer electrons sit farther out, and atoms grow.

P5.text: Size and pull. Almost every trend comes from these two.

S1.text: Let's light up the table, one trend at a time. First, atomic radius.

S2.text: It shrinks across a period, from lithium at one hundred and fifty two picometres to fluorine at sixty four. It grows down a group, up to caesium at two hundred and sixty two.

S3.text: Second, ionization enthalpy, the energy needed to pull an electron out of an atom. It rises across a period, from lithium at five hundred and twenty to neon at two thousand and eighty one kilojoules per mole. It falls down a group.

S4.text: Third, electron gain enthalpy, the energy change when an atom takes in an electron. It becomes more negative across a period, and less negative down a group.

S5.text: Fourth, electronegativity, the pull on a shared pair. It rises across a period, and falls down a group. Fluorine is the top, at four.

S6.text: Fifth, metallic character. Metals lose electrons easily. So metallic character falls across a period, and rises down a group.

B1.text: Notice the pattern. Radius and metallic character grow towards the bottom left. The other three grow towards the top right.

B2.text: Pause and think. Which is more metallic, potassium or magnesium?

B3.text: Potassium! It sits further left and further down. Both moves make an element more metallic.

D1.text: Now, why are the two ends of a period the most reactive? Step by step.

D2.text: Step one. On the far left, ionization enthalpy is the lowest. Alkali metals lose one electron easily, and form positive ions, called cations.

D3.text: Step two. On the far right, electron gain enthalpy is the most negative. Halogens take an electron easily, and form negative ions, called anions.

D4.text: Step three. In the middle, atoms neither lose nor gain electrons easily. So reactivity is lowest in the centre.

D5.text: Step four. Noble gases have full shells. Their electron gain enthalpy is positive, so they hardly react at all.

T1.text: Remember this. Small atoms pull hard. Big atoms let go easily. Every trend follows from that.

W1.text: Now, one worked example, with oxides.

W2.text: Using water, show that sodium oxide is basic and that dichlorine heptoxide is acidic.

W3.text: N a two O plus water gives two N a O H. Sodium hydroxide, a strong base.

W4.text: Count the atoms. Sodium, two and two. Oxygen, two and two. Hydrogen, two and two. Balanced.

W5.text: C l two O seven plus water gives two H C l O four. Perchloric acid, a strong acid.

W6.text: Count again. Chlorine, two and two. Oxygen, eight and eight. Hydrogen, two and two. Balanced.

W7.text: Litmus paper confirms it. The base turns red litmus blue. The acid turns blue litmus red.

C1.text: Across period three, the oxides change step by step. The oxide on the far left is the most basic. The one on the far right is the most acidic.

C2.text: In the middle, aluminium oxide is amphoteric. It behaves as an acid with bases, and as a base with acids.

C3.text: And some oxides, like carbon monoxide, nitric oxide and nitrous oxide, are neutral. They are neither acidic nor basic.

X2.text: Students think more electrons means a bigger atom. So they say the radius grows across a period.

X3.text: But across a period, the extra electrons go into the same shell, and the extra protons pull them in. The radius shrinks.

E1.text: Where is this asked? NEET asks order questions on radius, ionization enthalpy and metallic character. JEE Main asks statement questions on the same trends.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Which of these orders is correct? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. Fluorine, oxygen, nitrogen, carbon.

A2.text: Electronegativity rises across period two. Four, three point five, three, two point five.

A3.text: A is reversed. Radius grows down a group, so fluorine is the smallest.

A4.text: B is wrong, sodium is further left than magnesium, so it has the lower ionization enthalpy. And D is reversed too, metallic character falls across a period.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why does atomic radius shrink across a period?

Y3.text: Two. Which is more metallic, sodium or aluminium, and why?

Y4.text: Three. Why are the two ends of a period the most reactive?

N1.text: Next time: why does boron break the ionization enthalpy trend, and why does chlorine beat fluorine? We find out in exceptions and anomalous periodic behaviour.
